profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting between the platform security workstream and the developer productivity workstream at a SaaS company that is piloting SecDocker in its GitHub Actions-based CI pipeline. The company already runs builds and tests in Dockerized runners for 40 microservices, and SecDocker is being introduced as a transparent policy-enforcement layer to harden container execution in CI without noticeably increasing release latency. The immediate context is that a shared integration branch will be cut next week for three high-traffic services, so the teams need to align on the interface between the SecDocker policy bundle and the existing CI templates. The agenda is to confirm what artifact the security team will hand off, how the application teams will consume it in workflows, what 'green' rollout status means for next week's integration checkpoint, and who updates the shared exception list for containers that need temporary allowances. The expected outcome is surface-level agreement on the handoff package, rollout timing, status reporting, and ownership of the exception mechanism across the two workstreams.

members.name: Nina Alvarez
members.expertise: Container hardening, CI/CD security controls, policy-as-code, GitHub Actions runner security
members.background: Nina joined from a cloud security startup and now leads rollout of preventive controls across internal engineering platforms; she has recently finished the first SecDocker policy bundle and wants downstream teams to adopt it with minimal back-and-forth.
members.private_state: She wants the pilot to look operationally smooth and to avoid reopening policy details before the security review, while quietly minimizing custom exceptions that could weaken the control model.
hidden_assumptions: When she says the 'baseline policy,' she means the signed SecDocker rule bundle plus its default deny/allow templates stored in the central security-policy repository.
A service is 'green' once its default CI path completes under enforced policy for the main branch and the weekly scheduled build, even if uncommon workflow branches are not yet exercised.
The 'exception list' is a centrally owned YAML in the security-policy repository that application teams can request changes to but should not edit directly.
Teams will consume the policy through the reusable GitHub Actions workflow wrapper, not by invoking the SecDocker container directly in each repository.

members.name: Ethan Brooks
members.expertise: CI template maintenance, build tooling, monorepo integration, release engineering
members.background: Ethan maintains the shared GitHub Actions templates used by product teams and is responsible for keeping build times stable and reducing friction when new platform requirements are introduced.
members.private_state: He wants to absorb SecDocker into existing templates with as little service-team retraining as possible, and he is concerned that hidden central dependencies will create release-week bottlenecks.
hidden_assumptions: When he hears 'baseline policy,' he means the minimum per-repository configuration file and sample rules each service needs to commit locally so template adoption is self-contained.
A service is 'green' if the standard pull-request pipeline passes on the representative services in the pilot set without materially increasing median CI time.
The 'exception list' is a repo-adjacent configuration file managed by the owning service team, because exceptions are usually tied to local build quirks.
Integrating SecDocker means adding one step inside the existing build job in the shared CI template, not routing services through a separate reusable workflow.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the baseline policy
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they will roll out the 'baseline policy' next week.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the centrally maintained signed SecDocker policy bundle and default templates delivered from the security-policy repository.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a lightweight per-repository starter config that each service checks into its own repository and can version with its CI template.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In platform work, 'baseline policy' naturally sounds like a shared starting point to both sides, so each hears a familiar implementation model behind the same phrase and sees no reason to restate the packaging details.

misalignment_points.topic: What green means for rollout status
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that the pilot services should be 'green' before the integration branch is cut.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means enforced-policy success on main-branch builds and the scheduled nightly run for each pilot service, showing the control works in default and unattended execution paths.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means pull-request builds for the representative pilot services pass with acceptable runtime impact, which is sufficient to declare rollout readiness.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Status colors like 'green' are routinely used as shorthand in coordination meetings, and both participants assume the other is using the team's usual status language rather than a different operational acceptance threshold.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss keeping the 'exception list' updated during rollout.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the exception list is a single central artifact owned by platform security; service teams can request additions, but governance and edits stay with her team.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes each service team owns its own exception entries in a local config file, while his team only provides template hooks and guardrails.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both support the same apparent process outcome—exceptions will be updated when needed—so the deeper question of whether the artifact is centralized or distributed remains implicit and feels too operationally obvious to spell out.

misalignment_points.topic: How SecDocker will be wired into CI
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that developer productivity will 'hook SecDocker into the shared template.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects Ethan's team to call the security-owned reusable workflow that wraps build steps with SecDocker enforcement and standardized logging.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects to add a direct SecDocker invocation step inside the current shared build job so the existing template structure stays intact.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'hook into the shared template' sounds implementation-neutral and routine; both think they are simply confirming integration ownership, not choosing between materially different execution paths.

turns.inner_thought: I want this to feel straightforward: security hands off the signed SecDocker bundle from the central security-policy repo, Dev Productivity wires it in through the reusable workflow wrapper, and we avoid reopening policy semantics. If I keep this at the handoff and readiness level, we can get to the integration branch next week without inviting custom carve-outs.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I want to use this to lock down what security is handing off for SecDocker, how it meets the shared CI path, and what we need in place before next week's integration branch for the three pilot services.

turns.inner_thought: My goal is to absorb this into the existing template with minimal disruption. If I can add SecDocker inside the current shared build job, teams won't have to learn a new workflow shape, and we can keep release week stable. I just need a package I can fan out repo by repo without central coupling slowing us down.
turns.utterance: Yep, that's the right scope from my side. I mainly want to make sure we can hook SecDocker into the shared template for the three pilots without creating churn for the service teams or adding release-week risk.

turns.inner_thought: The baseline policy is ready enough by Wednesday: the signed rule bundle plus default deny/allow templates in the central repo. Once Ethan points the template at the reusable workflow, I just need main and the scheduled weekly run to pass under enforcement for each pilot. That is green enough for security review, and I don't need to discuss odd branches yet.
turns.utterance: From security, I can hand over the baseline policy by Wednesday. If we get it wired in on that timeline, the pilot services should be green before the integration branch is cut.

turns.inner_thought: Wednesday is fine. If I get the baseline policy then, I can push the starter config into the three pilot repos and validate in PR runs. If those representative services stay fast and passing through Friday, I'll call that green and we can cut the branch with confidence.
turns.utterance: Wednesday works for me. I can fan the baseline policy into the pilot repos and use PR runs to make sure everything is green by Friday.

turns.inner_thought: Good. He'll hook SecDocker into the shared template by calling the security-owned reusable workflow, and that keeps enforcement and logs standardized. I do not want services invoking the container ad hoc or drifting from the wrapper before review.
turns.utterance: That lines up well. Developer productivity can hook SecDocker into the shared template, and my team will keep the logging and enforcement behavior consistent across services.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect—I'll just add one more step in the current build job and preserve the template shape everybody already uses. If the service teams barely notice the change, that's a win. I assume her team just means they'll keep the tool behavior stable while I wire the step in.
turns.utterance: That fits my plan. I only need one extra step in the current build job, and that should let us preserve the existing template shape for the service teams.

turns.inner_thought: Some teams will hit temporary allowances, especially around specific containers. That's fine as long as changes flow through the centrally owned exception YAML and stay tightly governed. I want to signal responsiveness without implying local edits are okay.
turns.utterance: One other thing: a few builds may need temporary entries in the exception list early on. We can keep that updated quickly during the first week of rollout if anything comes up.

turns.inner_thought: Makes sense. I'll tell the pilot teams to manage their repo-side exception list as they discover local quirks—image pulls, sidecars, whatever trips the new check. That keeps fixes close to the owning teams and avoids a central bottleneck.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I'll let the pilot teams know to keep their exception list current if any image pulls or sidecar containers need allowances.

turns.inner_thought: For my status reporting, I need clean unattended execution too, not just a happy-path PR. Once the nightly run is clean on all three services under enforced policy, I can confidently tell the security review thread the pilot is green.
turns.utterance: And just so we're aligned on status reporting, once the nightly run is clean on the three services, I'll report the pilot as green to the security review thread.

turns.inner_thought: I'll track what matters on my side: PR stability and CI time. If the representative repos hold steady after the template change and don't slow people down, that's green enough for rollout readiness. Her note about the nightly run sounds fine as an additional signal.
turns.utterance: Makes sense. I'll watch PR turnaround time after the template change, and I expect to mark the pilot green as soon as the representative repos stay stable.

turns.inner_thought: I'll send the signed bundle references and the reusable workflow materials right away. If I package it cleanly, Ethan can plug in without asking to tweak the policy itself. The less we debate internals before review, the better.
turns.utterance: Great. I'll send over the baseline policy package and the reusable integration materials right after this meeting so your team can start on the handoff.

turns.inner_thought: Good, I have what I need: update the shared template, notify service owners, and keep exceptions maintained near the repos while we validate in PR. If all three pilots stay stable by Friday, we'll be in good shape for the branch cut.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I'll update the shared template, notify the service owners about exceptions, and aim for a green pilot before Friday.
